title: Chapter 201 – The Source
html:
[Bell's Surgery and the Council Chamber – Lin Jian]

The Archivist does not sit down to say it, and that is how Jian knows it is worse than he thought.

Perrin Ado stands at the foot of Little Mei's cot with his hands behind him and his black eyes fixed on a point just above the child's head. He is a lean, hard-edged man, six hundred years out of his century, wrapped in a gray blanket that Qinghe has pinned at the shoulder with a kitchen skewer. He has the manner of someone who has been trained to read a ledger aloud to a room that does not wish to hear it. He has not touched the bread Bell left for him. He has not looked at anyone's face.

"I will say it plainly," he says. "Because I have found that kindness, in this matter, only makes the hearing longer."

"Say it," says Jian.

He sits on a stool by the wall with his staff across his knees. The surgery is crowded. Bell is at the bedside. Tian Mo kneels beside her, his stone hand still pulsing a faint green on the small rib cage. Hua stands against the shelves with Mo Yan pressed to her side. Mei, a pale unsteady shimmer, floats near the head of the cot, and her hand hovers an inch above her sister's hair, not touching it.

"The Quiet Remedy was never a pill," says Perrin Ado. "Nor a tonic. It was a pattern, written into a living body, which taught that body to correct its own blood. The medics held it as a craft. Four hundred and seventy-three of them, each with a different fragment, each unable to cure alone. When they slept in Ring One, the fragments were kept apart. To use the remedy, you had to wake them together."

"And they are gone."

"Yes. Their fragments are gone." He draws a breath. "But the Warden made a second keeping. In the children. She did not copy the whole. She copied it in eight pieces, one to a child, so that no one child could ever be used as a weapon, or a ransom, or a spare part."

"Eight pieces," says Hua, from the shelves.

"Each of the Eight carries a fragment. The Seven you know. The eighth..." His gaze moves, at last, to Jian, and holds. "The eighth is you, Head Lin. The Roll says so. The Warden marked you first."

Jian does not flinch. He has had a week with this. He has turned it over in the dark, a smooth hard fact like a stone from a riverbed. "And the ninth?"

"There is no ninth. The Warden would not make a ninth." Perrin's mouth tightens. "Your Mei is not of the line. She is the Founder's own daughter, and her blood carried the fault, but she died before the remedy was made. She has no fragment. She cannot give one."

Mei makes a small sound.

"I'm sorry," says the Archivist, and for the first time there is something almost human in his voice. "I did not wish to say it in front of you."

"It's all right." The voice is very quiet. "I knew. I didn't know I knew."

* * *

The method is simple, and that is what makes it terrible.

Perrin lays it out on Bell's worktable with a stub of charcoal and a sheet of brown paper, quickly, in a clerk's tidy hand. Eight small circles in a ring. A ninth at the center, marked with a cross. A line from each of the eight to the center.

"To cure the child," he says, "the eight fragments must be brought together in the vessel. That is the whole of it. A single body that receives all eight at once will have the remedy complete. The fault will correct. She will live."

"Brought together how?" says Bell. Her voice is level. She has not looked up from the pulse she is counting.

"Two ways." Perrin taps the paper. "The first is the old way. A graft. Marrow, drawn from each of the eight, mingled in a vessel and given to the child by the mouth. It is crude. It works. It costs each donor a season of life, and leaves the tremor worse."

"How much worse?"

"Both hands, in time. Then the knees." He does not soften it. "It would not kill them. It would not be pleasant."

Nobody answers.

"The second way is the Interface's." He turns the charcoal over in his fingers. "I am told you have one, Head Lin. I am told it prints. The Ring is a template bank. If the eight fragments are read from the eight bodies, they can be joined in the template, and a copy printed for the child, without drawing a drop from anyone."

"It would cost," says Jian.

"Everything costs."

"What would this cost?"

"I do not know the Interface." The Archivist meets his eyes. "I know the Ring. A full copy of the Remedy is large. The Ring would carry it as a weight. Nine holders, one weight, shared evenly. But the Ring is not even, is it? I have watched the girl all day. She gives, and gives, and does not take."

"Mei," says Jian, very low.

"I know," says Mei. "I did the sum."

"What sum?"

"If you print it through the Ring, I'd have to carry it." Her smile is thin and brave and terrible. "I'm the keystone. I carry what's left over. And I'm at six and a half percent."

"It would not kill you," says Perrin. "Not at once. But you would not wake for a season."

"And the Hall?"

"Would sleep." He says it flat. "The Nine are the Hall's pulse. If the weakest sleeps, the others carry her. For a season, perhaps longer."

A silence falls, so complete that Jian can hear the fire.

* * *

The Nine meet in the Council Chamber at noon, and no one raises a voice.

That is the worst of it. He has braced for shouting. He has braced for Duan Ke to throw a chair, for Zhen Li to cry, for Cheng Hui to say, in his careful, courteous voice, that this is a matter for the Elders. None of it comes. They sit in their chairs round the table of unmarked stone with their hands folded, nine children and the stool with the firewood back, and they look at one another in a stillness so profound it has weight.

"I'll do it," says Duan Ke.

"You will not," says Hai Ren.

"I'm the oldest after Cheng Hui. I'm the strongest. I'm the one who can be spared."

"No one can be spared."

"I can." The boy's scarred face is hard. "I'm no use to anyone, and you know it. I can't read. I can't speak in council. I'm only good for fighting, and there's no more fighting to be done." His voice cracks. "Let me do it. Let me be the one who gave."

"That is not a reason," says Cheng Hui gently.

"It's the only one I have."

"It is not." Hai Ren has risen. She stands with her hands flat on the table and her eyes blazing. "Do you hear yourself? You think the price of being useful is to give up your knees? That isn't how it works. That's how they made us. Be quiet, be useful, be kept. I will not do it again. Not to you."

Duan Ke stares at her. His mouth works. Then, slowly, he sits down, and covers his face with both hands.

Jian watches. He has not spoken. He is listening, as he learned to listen in the Wall, to what is under the voices. And what is under them is fear: not of pain, not even of death, but of being asked to prove that they are worth keeping.

We are alike, he thinks. All of us.

"I have a question," says Zhen Li.

She is eleven, and shy, and she bites her nails to the quick. She has never spoken first in a council. They turn to look at her, and she flushes to the roots of her hair.

"Is there a third way?" she says. "The Archivist said two. But I think..." She swallows. "I think there's usually a third."

"Go on."

"The Interface prints from templates. But it can read, too. It can scan." Her eyes are huge. "If it scanned one of us, one single person, who held a fragment... could it print the other seven from the one?"

The room goes very still.

"The Remedy is eight pieces," says Cheng Hui slowly. "But the pieces fit. They were made to fit. If one is whole, it should hold the shape of the rest."

"It is not guaranteed," says Jian.

"But is it possible?"

He sits back. His hand is trembling on the head of the staff. Slowly, he opens the panel at the edge of his mind and puts the question, plainly, with no ornament.

Could one carrier be the template for all eight?

He reads it three times. His mouth is dry.

The anchor. He thinks of Hua in the corridor, kneeling, saying the name of her daughter. He thinks of a woman writing I do not know whether I have done right, and meaning it, and doing it anyway.

She picked me, he thinks, because she knew I would say yes.

"Jian," says Mei.

"Yes."

"You have the face."

"What face?"

"The one you make when you've already decided." Her gray eyes are steady. "Say it. Don't make us ask."

He looks round the table. At Duan Ke with his hands over his face. At Hai Ren, white and furious. At Cheng Hui, gravely waiting. At the faint small shimmer of the girl who held a door for a hundred years and asks nothing now but the truth.

"There is a way," he says. "I would be the source. A single source, no draw on the Ring. It would cost me ten years and a good deal of what Bell has just mended." He swallows. "And I would not argue about it."

"No," says Hai Ren.

"Hai Ren—"

"No." She is shaking. "You've given enough. You've given more than anyone. You're coughing blood. You've printed yourself twice. I will not sit here and vote to let you spend ten more years of a life that's already running out."

"It is not yours to vote."

"It is." Her voice breaks. "You said it yourself. We share. That's the whole of what we are."

Jian says nothing. He cannot. He looks down at the stone table and sees, with a clarity that surprises him, the faint scratches left by six hundred years of hands. Nine seats. Nine sets of knuckles. One long, patient argument about what it means to carry.

"Then vote," he says quietly. "Not on whether I should. On whether you will let me."

* * *

They vote with their hands, again, and it is not unanimous.

He has expected that. It is almost a relief. Four hands rise slowly: Cheng Hui, Zhen Li, Tao, and Ao, who has no idea what is happening and holds his up because Tao does. Four stay down. Hai Ren sits with her arms folded, glaring. Duan Ke is staring at the floor. Mo Yan is looking at her mother, and her mother is looking at the table.

Mei votes last.

She lifts her small silver hand. It shakes. The light of her face is so faint that Jian can see the stone wall through it. For a long moment the hand hangs in the air, and she looks at him, only at him, with her old gray eyes.

"I vote yes," she says. "But I want to say why."

"Say."

"Because I can't." Her voice cracks. "I'm the only one who can't. I wasn't made with a fragment. I don't have anything to give. All I can do is sit here and watch you spend your life, and it's the worst feeling I've ever had." She wipes her face. "So I'm going to give you the only thing I do have. My vote. And I'm going to say it out loud, so nobody can say you did it alone."

Jian looks at her. His throat has closed.

"Five," says Cheng Hui softly.

"Four, then four," says Hai Ren. "No. It isn't settled."

"It is." Duan Ke has lifted his head. His eyes are red and furious. He is staring at Jian as though he would like to strike him. "It's settled. Because I'm not going to be the one who says no and watches her die." His hand goes up, slowly, stiffly. "Six."

"Duan Ke—"

"Shut up, Hai Ren," says the boy, without heat. "Just this once."

Hai Ren's face crumples. She puts her head down on the stone table and her shoulders shake, and no one touches her. No one needs to. After a moment her hand lifts, blindly, and joins the others in the air.

"Seven," says Cheng Hui.

Mo Yan raises hers. Hua, against the wall, does not vote. She has no seat. But Jian sees her hand close tight round the mark on her palm, and the faint glow of it flickers and steadies.

"Nine," says Cheng Hui. His voice breaks. "It's carried."

* * *

Little Mei's first question, when she wakes, is not about the fever.

"Where's Mr. Ear?" she says, sitting bolt upright, with her hair on end.

"Under your chin."

"Oh." She finds him, checks his single ear, and relaxes. "Good. I thought I'd lost him." She scans the room, solemn and unhurried: the cots, the bag of herbs, Tian Mo's stone hand on the bedpost, the small silver shape on the pillow. "Mei."

"I'm here."

"I'm sorry I lent you the thing."

"You didn't know."

"I know now." The brown eyes fill. "You said it cost, and I said I had lots. I was wrong."

"You were five," says Mei. "It's allowed."

"Are you cross?"

"Very."

"How cross?"

"Cross enough to put you in socks until spring," says Mei, and the child laughs through her tears, and Mei, who has not been able to hold anyone for a hundred years, pulls the small body against her and does not let go.

* * *

Pebble waits for him in the corridor, as he knew she would.

She sits on the cold floor outside the Council Chamber with her bronze scales fluffed against the draft, and when he comes out she does not rise. She watches him with her black bead eyes. He walks past her, three steps, four, and stops.

Yes, he says. I know.

The thought comes through the bond like a stone dropped in water. You are going to make yourself smaller.

"A little."

You are going to make me smaller. Every time. I have counted. She uncurls and climbs, with deliberate, scratchy dignity, up the length of his staff, over his arm, and onto his shoulder. There will be nothing left to take up the stair.

"There will be enough."

How much is enough?

He is silent. She presses her cold nose against the hollow of his neck.

Your mother's tea is on the table, she says, with the dry, practical air of one who has decided an argument is over. Drink it before it goes cold.

He laughs. It rattles in his chest. He lets her stay.

* * *

Bell does it at dusk, in the surgery, with the fire built high and the door barred.

It is a strange procedure. Nothing is cut. Nothing is drawn. Jian lies on his back on the second cot with a clean cloth across his forehead and Bell's dry fingers on his wrist, and the Interface, in the corner of his sight, counts down in small plain letters. Across the room Little Mei lies under her quilts, fever-bright, her lips parted, and Tian Mo kneels beside her with his stone hand on her heart.

It takes six hours. He remembers the first two. After that the world goes soft and far away, like a house seen from the end of a long road, and the voices in it blur: Bell's, counting; Yue's, from the foot of the cot, saying his name; Mei's, high and clear, singing something with no words. He drifts. He thinks of his mother's hands. He thinks of a Wall in the snow, and a boy at a desk with a slate, writing STAND AT THE BACK. He thinks, quite distinctly, that it is a good thing to be an anchor, if one is going to be a weight at all.

At some point there is a pain in his right hand, sudden and sharp. He cannot lift his head to see. He knows what it is.

He opens his eyes. The room is dim. The fire has burned low. Across the surgery, in the next cot, a small brown head moves on the pillow, and a thin piping voice says, quite clearly, in the tone of one who has woken from a very long nap:

"I'm hungry."

Bell makes a sound that is half sob and half laugh. Tian Mo's stone hand lifts from the child's chest. Mei gasps, and then she is laughing too, and crying, and everyone in the room is saying something at once. Jian lies on his back and stares at the ceiling, and does not trust himself to speak, and lifts his right hand into the firelight.

It trembles. It trembles like a leaf. He watches it, for a long time, and thinks that it is the hand of a man who has chosen well enough.

* * *

Yue is sitting on the edge of his cot when he wakes the second time, and she does not pretend to have just arrived.

It is long after midnight. The surgery is dark except for a single lamp. Across the room Little Mei sleeps, flushed and peaceful, with Mr. Ear tucked under her chin and Mei curled in a thin silver crescent on the pillow beside her. Bell snores in the corner chair, a small round shape under a quilt. The fire has sunk to embers.

"You promised," says Yue, very quietly.

"I did."

"You said you would tell me when it was a thing you could put into words without making it worse." She does not look at him. She is looking at his right hand, where it lies on the blanket, trembling. "You said you swore it."

"I did."

"Is it a thing you can put into words yet?"

He considers. His throat is dry. He thinks of a thing in his head that was built for nine hosts and has only one, and of a world that no longer exists, and of how many ways there are to say a true thing so that it breaks the person who hears it.

"Not all of it," he says. "Not yet. But some."

"Say some."

"I am not hiding anything that will hurt you." He chooses each word. "I am hiding it because it is not finished. When it is finished, you will be the first. Before Mother. Before the Nine."

"That is not an answer."

"It is the one I have."

Yue studies him for a long time. The lamp makes her bandaged hand a pale smear in her lap.

"I knew you were not the brother who left at nine," she says at last, very quietly. "I have known since the courtyard. He would have cried at the funeral. You counted the names." Her eyes are bright and fierce. "I do not need to know what you are. I need to know you will tell me before you do something I cannot forgive."

"I will."

"Swear it."

"I swear it." The words come easily. "Again."

She takes his trembling hand in both of hers. "And you have been the best brother I have ever had, and I have had only two. So do not die of something stupid."

He cannot answer. He turns his hand in hers, and she holds it, and for a long time neither moves.

"Thank you," he says.

"You may thank me by living," says Yue. "Ninety-three years. I have checked with Bell, who checked with the thing you will not tell us about, and it is a good deal longer than most."

"You asked Bell to ask?"

"I asked Mei to ask. Mei asked the lamps. The lamps are not as discreet as you think." Her smile is small and sharp. "This clan has been keeping secrets for six hundred years, Jian. We are very bad at it."

He lets his head fall back on the pillow. The ceiling is brown with old smoke. For the first time in weeks, nothing in his chest hurts, and nothing in his head is counting.

He laughs, wetly, and she joins him. Across the room, Bell stirs in her chair and mutters something about people who could not let a woman sleep.

Cheng Hui is waiting in the corridor when Jian is finally allowed to leave.

He has been waiting for hours. The lamp beside him has burned down to a stub. He stands up as the door opens, tall and thin and grave, and for a moment neither of them speaks.

"She ate," says Cheng Hui. "Qinghe made her an egg."

"Good."

"She asked if she could go outside." His mouth twitches. "Barefoot."

"Let her."

"Qinghe said the same thing, and then made her wear socks." He laughs, helplessly. Then he stops, and his face changes. "Jian."

"Yes?"

"I wanted to say something." He is staring at Jian's hands, at the right one, trembling on the head of the staff. "I have the tremor too. I always have. It does not go away. But I have never minded it, because I thought it was a mark of what was wrong with me." He swallows. "It is not. It is the remedy. It is the thing that was put there to keep us alive."

"I know."

"You didn't, until yesterday."

"No."

"Neither did I." The boy straightens. "So I wanted you to know that I am not afraid of it any more. And I think the others will not be either. When they see yours."

Jian looks at him. At the long pale hands folded in front of the borrowed gown. At the faint fine tremor in the fingers, which he has always hidden, and does not hide now.

"A family trait," he says.

"The family's," says Cheng Hui. "And the Hall's. And the Nine's."

The corridor is very quiet. At the far end, a lamp flickers, and steadies, and goes on burning. Somewhere above them, on the hill, a tree is singing. It is not the lullaby. It is a plain bright tune with no words, climbing, like a child's, up a stair that does not stop.
